title: Why Church Membership Still Matters
subtitle: The biblical case for committed belonging, covenant membership, and accountability in a culture that treats church like a streaming service

sections.title: The Church You Can Cancel
sections.body:
We have made the church into a service you subscribe to and cancel. You attend when the music is good and the schedule allows. You leave the moment it costs you something or someone disappoints you. You belong to nothing and call it freedom.

This is not the church the New Testament describes. It is a consumer arrangement wearing a cross.

Robert Bellah named this drift decades ago in his study of American individualism, the way we turned every institution, including the church, into a vendor of personal fulfillment we were free to abandon the instant it underdelivered. The result is a Christianity with no skin in the game. We have congregations full of attenders and starved for members, full of people who consume the church and empty of people who have committed to it. The question is not whether this is comfortable. It plainly is. The question is whether it is the thing Jesus died to build. It is not.

sections.title: There Is No Unattached Christian
sections.body:
The New Testament does not imagine a believer who belongs to no congregation. It does not have a category for it. When Paul writes, he writes to bodies, and a body part severed from the body is not free. It is dead.

You were not saved into a private spirituality. You were baptized into a people. The pronoun of the New Testament is overwhelmingly you plural.

Membership is just the honest name for that belonging made visible and accountable. It is the church saying these are the ones we have committed to watch over, and the believer saying these are the ones I have committed to be known by. The early church kept lists for a reason. They knew who their widows were. They knew who had been excluded and who had been restored. They knew their own. To say I love the universal church but will commit to no actual congregation is to love an abstraction and refuse a neighbor. It is the religious version of loving humanity while being unable to live with anyone.

sections.title: Belonging That Can Cost You
sections.body:
Membership matters precisely because it is costly. It commits you to people you did not choose and would not have chosen, and that is the point, not the problem.

Anyone can love a church they can leave. Covenant is love that has shut the exit, so that staying becomes a discipline and not a mood.

The people God gives you in a local church will irritate you, fail you, vote differently, parent differently, and sit too close. And staying anyway, bound to them by a commitment that does not flinch when they disappoint you, is one of the few places left in modern life where a person actually learns to love. You cannot be sanctified by people you are free to abandon the moment they cost you something. The friction is the furnace. We avoid membership not because we doubt its theology but because we know what it will ask. It will ask us to stay when leaving would feel better. That is exactly what it is for.

sections.title: Submitting to Being Known
sections.body:
Membership also means submitting to oversight, and that word has gone bitter in our mouths for good reason. Authority has been abused, and many have fled accountability because the only accountability they ever saw was control.

But the answer to abused authority is not no authority. It is healthy authority, which is shepherding, not domination.

To be a member is to say to a body of elders, you have permission to know me, to ask after my soul, to come when I wander. The writer of Hebrews tells leaders they will give an account for the souls in their care, and tells the people to make that a joy and not a burden. Neither sentence makes sense without committed membership. A pastor cannot give an account for a soul he was never permitted to know. The wandering Christian who answers to no one is not free. He is unprotected. Being known is the safety we keep mistaking for a threat.

sections.title: What the Church Owes Its Members
sections.body:
Let me turn the indictment where it belongs. If members owe the church commitment, the church owes its members something the consumer model never required of it.

It owes them actual care. A membership roll that is only a list of donors is its own kind of fraud, and pastors have run that fraud for years.

We have asked people to commit to congregations that would not have noticed if they vanished. We have demanded loyalty and offered anonymity in return. That is on us. So if we are going to make the case for membership, and we should, we had better build the kind of church worth being a member of. One that knows your name. One that shows up when you are sick. One that comes after you when you drift. Membership is a two way covenant or it is a manipulation. Done right, it is the most countercultural thing a church can offer a lonely age. Not a service you consume. A people who have promised not to let go of you.
